utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Would the registrar please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, I ask that you bring in the accused. I see that has been done already. Very well. The interpreters, I would like to greet the interpreters. I hope they can hear me. Very well. And I see that the Prosecution is represented by whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Brenda Hollis, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the Defence is represented by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: George Vann, V-A-N-N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vann. Can the accused hear me? Can you hear me, Mr. Radic. Very well, the Chamber has come together for this public hearing in response to a request made by the accused, Mr. Radic, with regard to a personal matter. This is a very sad event dealing with a death in his family. This deals with a letter written to the president of the Tribunal, Mrs. McDonald, and this will be a matter which he will explain. Now, I have looked at this letter and I am in complete agreement, along with my colleagues. First of all, we will hear the request made by the Defence, then we will hear the impressions of the Prosecution, and then we ourselves will ask questions. So without further ado, Mr. Radic, will you please stand and please express -- by explaining in some detail this request that you sent to us on the 7th of July, 1998. Today is the 8th. So we received this letter yesterday evening, and we decided to meet today. Mr. Radic, I believe have you an interpreter there as well. Yes, I also salute you, Mr. Interpreter -- do you hear me, Mr. Interpreter? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am not interpreter for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, he is not getting the interpretation. Do you hear me Mr. Interpreter? Mr. Radic, do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you speaking to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I first -- I was first speaking to the interpreter to see whether the interpreter could hear me, and next after that I asked whether or not the accused can hear me, and I will ask first for the accused to address this Court, and then after that the Prosecution will make its comments to this Court, and then the Defence, the Defence counsel will then make its comments. Is everybody in agreement with that arrangement? Very well. I hope the interpreter understands which arrangements are being made because I understand the interpreters are to facilitate communication between the Defence Counsel and the accused. Does the accused hear me now? And does the interpreter hear me? Yes. Very well. Mr. Radic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yesterday around ten o'clock I talked on the telephone with my family and I was told that my older brother, Rajko, died. He was suffering from cancer. And so I was told this around 1.00. And around 2.00 I was -- asked -- submitted a request. Then I talked to my family and the burial was supposed to be at 2.00. They said that it could be postponed and I just wanted to be able to attend the funeral, if that is possible. I am going to sign anything that you need me to in terms of guarantees. I will come back. And I don't -- I also, I think that you may not be fully aware of the impact. If I went there, what echo that would have, what impact that would have back home. Because the impression is that those who go to The Hague never come back. I obviously cannot bring my brother back to life, but we were very close. We shared the same Courtyard. And that's all I have to say, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. Please be seated. Perhaps we will have other questions for you later on. I now turn to Brenda Hollis. Madam Prosecutor, what is your position on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, Your Honour, I know that it is not appropriate to speak directly to the accused, but I would like, through Your Honours, on behalf of the Prosecutor, to express to Mr. Radic her condolence on the passing of his brother. As to the merits of his application, Your Honour, we have no objection in principle to what Mr. Radic is requesting. Our one and only concern is that should this Chamber allow his request, that Mr. Radic be escorted and in custody with either personnel from this Tribunal or SFOR personnel or a combination during the time that he attends to this family matter. The Prosecutor assumes, without knowing, that Mr. Radic's brother -- the funeral will be in the Republika Srpska area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Based upon that assumption, we have general concerns were Mr. Radic be allowed to return there without having, what we believe would be necessary custodial and escort personnel with him. And that is the only concern that the Prosecutor has in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will have questions to ask you with regards to your proposal. Before continuing, I would like to turn now -- first of all, Madam Registrar, I understand the -- what the rules state with regards to provisional releases. Is there anything in the rules on detention that speak to this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, the detention rules do not have any special details about this type of case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is there no authorisation whatsoever for release in agreement with the host countries? Are there no provisions?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, the prison rules do not have any type of provisions in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vann.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am in complete accord with the statement made by the Prosecutor. I understand that to maintain security that he has to have the necessary protection from the Prosecutor's point of view, and any accommodations that could be made to ensure that the accused would be accompanied to his homeland to be present at his brother's funeral under appropriate safeguards and protection of this Court's jurisdiction, that he would safely return here, would be quite appropriate. And his family would appreciate that. And I think it would be to everybody's interest to have him present at his funeral. It would elevate this Court's sense of justice, it would probably remove some of the preconceived perceptions that the Serbs have -- that the people themselves have with regard to what the world may be doing to their people and not to others. Whether that perception is wrong or right, it's not my concern, but I appreciate this Court's -- anything this Court can do on the basis of decency and humanity to permit this man to go home to visit for the last time, perhaps, if he is convicted of these very serious charges. His mother and his family will not only have lost one brother, but they will probably never see the other brother again if these serious charges are proved beyond a reasonable doubt. And I would urge the Court to permit him to go to the funeral. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to turn to my colleagues. I believe you may have some questions to ask, either to the accused or either of the parties. Judge Rodrigues, do you have any questions you would like to ask? Would you like to ask them directly yourself? As you wish. First of all, the judges would like to return to the Prosecution and ask what the position of the Dutch government is. You know that in rule 65 it says that in exceptional circumstances, after hearing the host country, that the provisional release could be ordered. Have you been able to find the time to consult with the host country?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but I have to be able to say that I have not. We received this a very short time ago. I've been in trial today and I have not been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Madam Fauveaux, do you have any information.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the registry did contact the Dutch authorities and the Dutch authorities are aware of the request made by the accused, and the representative of the foreign affairs office, and its liaison in connection with this Tribunal says it has no objection to this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Now I allow my colleagues to ask their own questions. But, madam Prosecutor, once again I have a question for you. You talked about SFOR, but the SFOR mandate, would it allow them to, first of all, to protect the accused, because there could be some threats to the accused, but also would it allow to work with the and protect the investigators? The second question is could the Prosecution also send an escort of two investigators to accompany Mr. Radic to this funeral?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I may answer the second question first, Your Honour. Yes, the Prosecutor could and would send two investigators with this contingent. As to your first question, our position would, of course, be subject to approval by SFOR, because I cannot speak on their behalf. But I believe, based on cooperation that has existed in the past, that it is possible that such an arrangement could be made. It would be our position, again without committing us, for which I could not do, it would be our position that it would be within their general mandate in the country to assist in such a matter. But again, a very clear qualification that I cannot speak on behalf of the SFOR commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, perhaps in the next hour, do you think you perhaps might be able to put this question to SFOR so we can have a rapid solution to this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can certainly make our best efforts to talk to whomever we need to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. On behalf of my colleagues, once again, I would like to first of all turn to the accused. Mr. Radic, would you please stand. What type of guarantees would you bring to this Tribunal and that you will return to appear before this Court? Now, of course, the guarantees would be -- would come in the form of having someone accompanying you, but what kind of guarantees can you offer us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I say in front of these people that I will certainly come back here. And as far as my safety is concerned, I do not need one. Only if you feel that I do need. So I take responsibility to come back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. But your security is our concern, and we have to think about that, Mr. Radic. I don't know much about your case, because this is only the very start of the proceedings against you, but -- and there may be some people in your area, in your corner of the world where either they may be very good friends or very great enemies. Maybe you might have very great friends with whom you stay who perhaps you will never see again, but perhaps there might also be great enemies in the area who say you might turn us in. This is why we must also think about your safety. That's why we are thinking about that now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As far as your concerns, that is your business. But as far as I am concerned, I will take responsibility to come back, and I can sign any document to that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How is it that you were arrested, Mr. Radic? Did you surrender voluntarily or were you arrested by SFOR? How did that occur? One of the questions from my colleagues, and I am asking you now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, I did not surrender on my own. I was captured in front of my apartment, two date, three months ago. I was coming back from marketplace where I had borrowed some money in order to celebrate the Patron Saints Day. On that occasion my shoulder was broken. I have certain health problems stemming from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, were the circumstances violent?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is our understanding that they were not violent, that he was arrested. He did not voluntarily surrender, but other than what would typically go with an arrest where a person is seized, that there was no violence attendant to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, concerning the religious ceremony in your country, first of all, what religion is involved here, and what type of ceremonies is carried out? Because you said that the ceremony was or the funeral was to take place today. Will they be -- could they be postponed and will they be postponed? What type of ceremony? Please excuse me, but I don't know what type of ritual you carry out. Is this an orthodox tradition?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes. It is an orthodox ceremony and I was talking to my son around 3.00 when I received information that I would come here. And I told there that it was a possibility, but I said don't spread this around, don't turn it into an event, but just talk to the mother and to the brother's son, if you can. But if you can postpone it, fine. If I can make it, fine. If not, it would be a pity. It is my great wish and it is the last thing I can do for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to first consult with my colleagues. Ms. Hollis, my colleagues would like to know what kind of guarantees, concrete guarantees, you, yourself would be asking for and what type of contact you think that he might have with -- whether there could be any problems as far as any kind of witnesses in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The guarantees that we would request, and believe would be appropriate, would be that Mr. Radic would go under 24-hour escort and custody. We believe that that would be appropriate to diffuse or to build a, perhaps a prohibition in those who may want to take this occasion, an occasion of sorrow, but perhaps could also bring to the fore some other people's anger about what they may have considered an unfair arrest and removal from the territory. And we believe, however, that with an appropriate escort that those feelings may exist, but would not be evidenced in any type of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would just like to understand, in a more explicit way what you meant by 24-hour escort and custody. You mean to say that you will go only for 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What do you mean by custody in that case?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I mean is that throughout the period he is gone from the detention centre, he will be accompanied on a 24-hour basis by escort personnel, for whatever period this Chamber may determine to allow him to be gone. And custody, I simply mean he would be in the custody and in the care of the personnel who compose the escort, whatever that final composition is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that imply that he does not meet anybody, if he's in custody, he cannot meet other people who come to see him?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He can?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It would simply be that he would be accompanied at all times by escorts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The escorts would be witnessing anything which has happening?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do these escorts understand Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe they would have to have an interpreter with them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you think the danger of any contacts which would interfere with the trial is out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We believe with an escort and with an interpreter that any such contact would be minimized. Can we ever totally eliminate such contact, if it's wished, we think not. But it could be minimized. And given the circumstance here, we believe that minimizing it would be sufficient to allow Mr. Radic to attend the last services for his brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And would you accept -- even to meet his family with an interpreter and with the -- with all these people around him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would ask that that be a condition of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you guarantee this condition?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can we guarantee?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, how do you know that once on the spot he would say no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Well, we believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are not part of the situation, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We believe, Your Honour, that since he would be there under the custody and control of the escort officers, that at such time as he said, "I no longer agree to those conditions," they would then bring him back, because he would have violated the conditions upon which he's being allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are confident that they could bring him back?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe that it's very likely they could. I believe, and the reason we are asking for an escort is that I don't believe that it's 100 percent certain that there would be a lack of any difficulties. And that's why I had mentioned some escort in conjunction with SFOR personnel. Because I believe were it Tribunal personnel alone, there is a not insignificant possibility that there could be difficulties. I think all of us must agree that though cooperation with authorities in that area is improving, certainly, I think at a minimum, we could say there is less than total cooperation. I believe we must also agree that there is some negative feeling in that area toward the Tribunal, and I believe all of those things would require a significant escort presence. And I believe that SFOR would, perhaps, add the significance to that escort presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said, perhaps, you are not yet sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I cannot speak on behalf of SFOR. So I don't know if they themselves would agree to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who can speak in their name?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The commanders that we will contact will be able to speak on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When do you expect an answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As the Presiding Judge had requested, as soon as this hearing is completed, I will go back to the Office of the Prosecutor and we will attempt to contact them forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, this is indeed a hearing. This is not a status conference. It is indeed a hearing. We are now going to adjourn and we are going to then have deliberation, but I would like to summarize -- let us admit, first of all, that there are no objections, in principle, from the Office of the Prosecutor, subject, of course, to the presence of an escort from the Tribunal, and at least an interpreter. Are you speaking of three people, perhaps three -- two investigators and a guard and an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the security personnel and the investigators would have to determine what an appropriate number would be. I would hesitate to speak about that before I consulted with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The second point is that the funeral may take place today, but we do not know for certain, but perhaps we would know and maybe perhaps this could be postponed until tomorrow. And the third point, and perhaps Mr. Radic, perhaps you don't know, but is there a means of having a quicker way of communicating with the area or, Mr. Vann, perhaps you know whether or not there is a fast means of communicating with the people in that area? Is it complicated to come in contact with the people there? For example, if he can only arrive until the day after tomorrow, then that would be -- we should know about this now. Have you been in consultation with your client about this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He's made arrangements. He fully expects that he can't come today, and the funeral has been postponed. He can arrange -- if it can be done within the reasonable future, he can postpone it, yes. The family will be willing to do that. And he has the authority. It just depends upon the conditions the Court can arrange for -- and whatever proper measures you need to obtain the consent of all of the people and as soon as possible. That's what he told me, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to have one point clear. He wants to go mainly for the purpose of the funeral? In other words, if the funeral is already done, would he still like to go? The funeral might take place today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Vann.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been instructed that he doesn't know whether the funeral has been postponed, but according to the religion, his orthodox religion, that if it has been -- if the funeral has been completed today, under their religion, the -- they have an obligation to visit the grave, the seven post-burial days. So he would like to go if the funeral is over, and perhaps, if the funeral has been postponed, then, of course, he would like to be present at the time of the funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Now, there are two essential points. One, depends on the Prosecution, the other depends on the accused. Now, can the accused find out whether or not the funeral can be postponed? That's something they perhaps can tell us as soon as possible, preferably. I want to know whether or not the registrar can facilitate in aiding the accused to make a telephone call.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. The accused has the right to use a telephone to contact family members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Radic. Immediately after this hearing, with the aid of your counsel, you will then contact your family members by phone, to find out whether or not this funeral can be postponed. And, of course, we have understood that the right is carried out over several days. But I've also understood from the question put to you by my colleague that we want to know whether or not you will be able to attend the funeral itself and to see whether or not we can accord this exceptional request. Please understand this context, but once again we hope that Mr. Radic will come back and tell us the truth. We trust that he will. We want for the truth to be told to us, and as for the -- as for Brenda Hollis's concern, it's important for us to find out whether or not SFOR will be able to give us some support, relative support. We are not asking for SFOR to be responsible for the escort itself, but we never know. Perhaps there might be some sort of incidence. Or at least have an escort to protect your investigators. If we can ask, perhaps, that SFOR aid us in this operation. I think -- it is now five o'clock. Let us see if we can obtain this information, which then will be given to the registrar as soon as possible. But for the time being the judges will deliberate and this will be based on these several hypotheses where one could be, let's say, that SFOR -- not escort necessarily, but oversee, if you will, the operations and also another option is that the funeral can be postponed to another time. This would be perhaps the most favourable possibility. And perhaps in the next hour to come we will foresee also the least favourable situation, in which SFOR cannot aid us in this operation and the funeral takes place today. Then perhaps you might find an intermediary hypothesis in which might be in between these two possibilities. I would like for the accused, however, to understand that he is here before a Tribunal which will try to do everything that it can to do to respect the emotional distress which the accused is going through, given the conditions in which his family is found now. At the same time, you should understand that this Tribunal shall not be ridiculed by an excuse made by the accused to go and see his family. And we hope that no difficulties will result in a decision made by this Tribunal. The hearing will reconvene in about 30 minutes. Will this be enough time to get some communication? Do you believe this is a good time period for our schedule? Because if it's possible to get an answer before, then I think that would be even better, but I think the accused can give us a response rather quickly

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I believe with regards to the accused, I believe the communication with his family could be done quite quickly. But with regards to the Prosecution, I know that she would do everything she can to join -- or to contact SFOR as soon as possible. This is also the concern that I have, because we should not go beyond the time period which we had already established within the work schedule of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, but here we are in exceptional circumstances and so it's necessary for each person to do something to try to respond to this issue before us. Let us say, then, that we shall -- judge Riad has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to request that when you contact SFOR, to give you a full view of the dangers to which the escort would be exposed, because this Tribunal is responsible for the escort also.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, judge Riad, for making that point. Judge Rodrigues, you have a point you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Hollis, I would like to know, also based on your information, whether or not any occurrences, whether any events have occurred in the last week which may have any impact on the security in that area. Perhaps I could be more explicit in my question if you do not understand me. But I think you perhaps know very well what type of occurrences I am speaking of that happen in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not aware personally of any incident that has occurred in the last week. However, when I speak with my interpreters, excuse me, with my investigators, I will further inquire into that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then the hearing will reconvene as soon as possible, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please bring the accused in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, with regard to the questions we put to you, and in particular the contact that you may have had in order to obtain some sort of guarantees so that the investigator is accompanying or escorting the accused to the funeral, could obtain some levels of guarantee for their security, what were you able to learn?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we re attempting contact with SFOR officials through our office in Sarajevo. At the time I came back down here to the Trial Chamber, I have no word as to what that contact is yet. In addition to that, Your Honour, our contact with SFOR, I believe in this matter, will have to go to a higher level of command to get an answer. We do not anticipate that we would have a full response from SFOR until later this evening. But those efforts are underway. It is my understanding, Your Honour, after talking with Mr. Vann, that in fact Mr. Radic's brother's funeral was held today, which would leave the request to visit the grave site within seven days, but would take some of the immediacy away from that request. The reason that I mention that is because the coordination, if SFOR were to agree to it, would probably take us into tomorrow or the day after. But at this moment I have nothing further to report to you in regard to the information you are requesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. So, for the time being, you cannot expect to have an answer from SFOR until tomorrow or the day after that. Mr. Radic, would you please stand. If I understood Madam Hollis correctly, the funeral took place today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, the burial did take place today. I just spoke to my son and the burial did take place in the course of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Please be seated. I think we are going to deliberation, but does the Prosecution have the same position with regards to the funeral? Since it took place today, does the Prosecution keep the same position? Is it still in favour of this provisional release or has this changed your position, given the fact that the funeral has taken place?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would hesitate to say that we are in favour of this provision. We do not oppose it in principle. It's our understanding, based on what has been indicated in the courtroom today that, because of orthodox religious beliefs, a visit to the burial site within seven days is also an important part of the funeral process. And, again, in principle, we are not opposed to that, assuming that we can put in place appropriate escort and custodial arrangements. And in that regard, Your Honours, I know you had asked if investigators could accompany the security personnel. I indicated that we believed we could, but I would hesitate to add that would not be in some type of security capacity. We would be relying on security personnel for that. It would rather be a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor who is familiar with the circumstances of the case and the surrounding circumstances regarding this accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to now turn to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What do you mean by security personnel? You say you may be relying on security personnel. You mean the SFOR or security personnel from here?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Whatever the arrangements would be, Your Honours. I mentioned earlier, we do not control the security personnel here. We do not control the SFOR. So our concern is that there be security personnel of sufficient quantity and type. How that would -- what that body would be constituted of, we don't know. Perhaps from the Tribunal with SFOR, perhaps SFOR. That would depend upon the position of the Tribunal in regards to what they would allow their security personnel to do and, of course, the position of SFOR in terms of what they would agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Tribunal will deliberate and will render its decision in the upcoming minutes in this room itself. The session is adjourned. We will resume as soon as we finish our deliberations. I believe this will be within the next 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Pursuant to Mr. Radic's request to attend the funeral of his brother, in a letter issued on the 7th of July, and following the hearing here on the 8th of July, the judges decide, taking note of the proposal made by the Prosecutor, who was not able to contact the SFOR authorities, and was unable to do so within the time period which will permit the judges to make a ruling on an issue which is of great urgence to enable the accused to attend the funeral, and also for the reasons that the funeral has already taken place, after having been informed of this by the accused, it stands, then, that the weight in the interests of this request for provisional release has been lost to a great degree. Even the fact there could be assistance given to a team going to the site of the funeral, this assistance could only be accessory to the actual movement. In conclusion, the judges have decided to reject the request of the accused for provisional release pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.
